feedback: If a learner denies that migration or echolocation is an adaptation because it 'isn't a body part', confirm all three kinds help survival and revisit the behavioural and physiological columns.
Ask learners to justify each placement by the defining feature of the category, not by the animal it belongs to.
If a card seems to span categories, treat it as a discussion point about what aspect is being classified rather than marking it simply right or wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptations are not only physical body parts; behaviours and internal/chemical processes are adaptations too, and reasoning about the KIND directs attention to the underlying category rather than a memorised definition.
learnerActions: Sort many real example cards into three columns: structural (body parts), behavioural (things the animal does), physiological (internal/chemical processes).

Place examples such as giraffe's long neck, eagle's talons and dolphin's streamlined body under structural; migration, hibernation and tool use under behavioural; antifreeze proteins in Arctic fish blood, bat echolocation and venom under physiological.
For each card, say WHAT KIND of adaptation it is and justify why (is it a body part, a behaviour, or an internal process?).
Flag any example you think belongs in more than one column and explain your reasoning.
activities.title: Sort real adaptations into three kinds

feedback: If a learner describes a feature without naming a problem, ask 'what problem in its environment does this solve?'
Reinforce that the same trait can be an advantage in one environment and a disadvantage in another, linking back to why selection depends on the environment.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Adaptation' means fit-to-environment — a feature that solves a specific survival problem in a particular setting — not just 'a cool feature'.
learnerActions: For several animals, pair a feature or behaviour with the specific survival PROBLEM and environment it addresses (e.g. streamlined body ↔ moving fast through water; hibernation ↔ surviving a season with little food).
For each pairing, name the environment and the problem explicitly, then state how the adaptation helps the animal survive and reproduce.
Compare two animals in different environments and explain why a trait that helps in one setting may not help in another.
activities.title: Match each adaptation to the survival problem it solves

feedback: If a learner expects one beak to win everything, point to the results: each tool is suited to a different food/niche.
Connect back to the sandbox: this variation in traits is exactly what the environment filters when it decides which individuals feed, survive and reproduce best.
Use predictions-then-measurement to surface and discuss any 'one best beak' assumption.
activities.intendedInsight: Different beaks win with different foods: varied traits are the raw material selection acts on, and the best trait depends on the environment, so there is no single 'best' design.
learnerActions: Use different tools as 'beaks' — e.g. tweezers, pliers, a spoon — and a mix of 'foods' such as dried seeds, rubber-band 'worms', and water.
Before timing, PREDICT which beak will collect the most of each food type.
Collect each food for a fixed time and record how much each beak gathered.
Compare predictions with results and identify which beak 'wins' with which food.
Explain what this shows about why varied beak shapes can each survive in different niches, and why no single beak is best at everything.
activities.title: Beaks-and-foods investigation: why varied traits survive in different niches

feedback: Target answer: 'That isn't how it works — stretching during one giraffe's life doesn't lengthen its babies' necks. In the past giraffes varied: some happened to have slightly longer necks. A common explanation is that those could reach more food, survived better and had more young, passing on the inherited variation for longer necks. Over many, many generations the average neck grew longer.' (Scientists also discuss other advantages of long necks; the key point is selection on inherited variation, not stretching.)

Lamarckian error (stretch then inherit the stretch): distinguish acquired changes, which are NOT inherited, from inherited variation selected over generations — a weightlifter's strong arms are not passed to their baby.
If a learner says a single animal remodels itself during its life, stress the change is in the POPULATION over generations, not in one animal.

If a learner says the animal 'decided' or 'tried' to adapt, replace intention with selection — variation already exists and the environment filters who survives and reproduces; there is no goal or will.

For hibernation: yes, it is an adaptation, usually classed as behavioural, though it also involves physiological changes such as lowered body temperature and heart rate — behaviours and internal processes help survival just as body parts do.
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptation arises across generations by natural selection on inherited variation: in a widely taught explanation, some giraffes happened to have slightly longer necks, those reached more food, survived better and had more young, so over many generations the average neck grew longer — distinct from an individual acquiring a trait by stretching and passing on what it gained.
learnerActions: Read this claim from a student: 'Giraffes got long necks because they kept stretching to reach higher leaves, and passed those longer necks on to their babies.'
Decide whether this is how it happened, and if not, explain how giraffes came to have long necks.

Answer probing follow-ups: Did ONE giraffe's neck get longer, or did giraffe necks get longer over generations — what's the difference? Where did the variation (some giraffes with longer necks than others) come from in the first place? A bodybuilder gets big muscles by training — will their baby be born with big muscles, and what does that tell us about how neck length is passed on?
Also decide: is hibernation an adaptation even though it isn't a body part? Why?
activities.title: The giraffe neck: diagnose and explain how the trait arose
